summary: IPv6 allows a packet to carry a Fragment Header without being split, which are called atomic fragments. Hosts typically send them after a Packet Too Big error advertises a small next-hop MTU. Some implementations treat them like normal fragments and may reassemble them with other queued fragments, which is risky. This document describes the problem and updates processing to avoid it.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a package gets a "may be in pieces" sticker even though it is whole. Some computers then wrongly mix it with other pieces. This fixes that.

questions: how should ipv6 handle atomic fragments
what is an ipv6 atomic fragment
how should ipv6 hosts process atomic fragments
why are ipv6 atomic fragments a security risk
subtitle: Why a whole IPv6 packet wearing a Fragment Header must never be mixed up with real fragments.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 packet can carry a Fragment Header without being split. Many hosts treated such "atomic fragments" like normal fragments, so an attacker could use forged fragments to disrupt otherwise unfragmented traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6946 updates RFC 2460 and RFC 5722 so that a packet with Fragment Offset 0 and the M flag 0 MUST be processed in isolation, and must not cause queued fragments to be discarded.
tldr.outcome: This removes the attack vector. The RFC updates RFC 2460 and RFC 5722.

today: RFC 6946 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2013. It updates RFC 2460 and RFC 5722, and its metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2460 lets IPv6 packets be fragmented to fit the Path-MTU. It also allows fragments to overlap, which makes reassembly ambiguous and could let attackers bypass firewall rules or evade intrusion detection systems. RFC 5722 forbids overlapping fragments: when overlap is detected, all fragments of that packet must be silently discarded.

RFC 6946 deals with a corner case. A packet can include a Fragment Header while not actually being fragmented. The RFC calls such a packet an atomic fragment. It can be handed to the upper-layer protocol without waiting for any other fragments, yet many implementations processed it as a regular fragment, reassembling it with any queued fragments sharing the same {IPv6 Source Address, IPv6 Destination Address, Fragment Identification}.
sections.eli5: A package with a "may be in pieces" sticker is sometimes just one whole package. Some computers still waited to glue it to other pieces, which let troublemakers mess things up.

sections.title: What Counts as an Atomic Fragment
sections.content:
The RFC defines IPv6 atomic fragments as IPv6 packets that contain a Fragment Header with the Fragment Offset set to 0 and the M flag set to 0. With offset 0 and no more fragments to follow, the packet is a single complete piece.

If an implementation instead tries to reassemble such a packet with other queued fragments, and an overlap occurs, an implementation that supports RFC 5722 will discard all of them. The RFC calls this an unnecessary vector for fragmentation-based attacks against non-fragmented traffic.
sections.eli5: If the sticker says "this is piece number zero and there are no more pieces," then the package is already whole.

sections.title: How Atomic Fragments Arise
sections.content:
Section 5 of RFC 2460 says that a host receiving an ICMPv6 "Packet Too Big" message with a Next-Hop MTU smaller than 1280 is not required to shrink its packets below 1280. It must, however, include a Fragment Header in later packets so an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator can pick a suitable Identification value. The RFC notes the payload may then have to be reduced to 1232 octets (1280 minus 40 for the IPv6 header and 8 for the Fragment header).

So any "Packet Too Big" message advertising a Next-Hop MTU below 1280 can trigger atomic fragments. A remote attacker can forge such a message. The attacker can then forge fragments with a matching address and identification tuple so that they are wrongly reassembled with legitimate fragments, causing packet drops and a possible denial of service.
sections.eli5: A forged "your packages are too big" note can trick a computer into adding the sticker to everything it sends. Then a troublemaker can slip fake pieces in.

sections.title: What Makes the Attack Easier
sections.content:
The RFC lists three factors that make things worse:

  • Many implementations do not validate received ICMPv6 error messages as recommended in RFC 4443 and documented in RFC 5927. For connectionless protocols, validation may be virtually impossible.
  • On receipt of such a message the Destination Cache (RFC 4861) is usually updated, so one forged message can affect multiple communication instances, such as several TCP connections, to that destination.
  • Some implementations use predictable Fragment Identification values, which greatly improves an attacker's chances.
sections.eli5: It is easier to cheat when nobody checks the notes, when one note changes how a computer treats everything it sends to someone, and when the pieces are numbered in a guessable order.

sections.title: The Required Processing Change
sections.content:
RFC 6946 updates Section 4.5 of RFC 2460 and Section 4 of RFC 5722. A host that receives a packet with a Fragment Header whose Fragment Offset and M flag are both 0 MUST process it in isolation from any other packets or fragments, even if they share the same address and identification tuple. The atomic fragment is "reassembled" from its own contents alone.

For that reassembly, the Unfragmentable Part is all headers up to, but not including, the Fragment Header. The Next Header of its last header comes from the Fragment Header's Next Header field. The Payload Length is the received Payload Length minus the Fragment Header length of 8.

Also, any fragments with the same tuple already in the reassembly queue MUST NOT be discarded when the colliding atomic fragment arrives, because atomic fragments MUST NOT interfere with normal fragmented traffic.
sections.eli5: The new rule: if a package is already whole, open it by itself. Never let it throw away pieces of some other package that is waiting to be put together.

sections.title: Survey of Operating Systems
sections.content: Appendix A reports a survey, tested on October 30, 2012, of whether popular operating systems generate atomic fragments in response to "Packet Too Big" messages advertising an MTU below 1280 bytes, and whether they implement this specification. For example, Linux 3.0.0-15, OpenBSD-current and Solaris 11 generated atomic fragments and implemented the specification, while FreeBSD 8.2, FreeBSD 9.0, Windows XP SP2, Windows Vista and Windows 7 Home Premium generated them and did not.
sections.eli5: The author checked which computer systems already followed the new rule. Some did, some did not yet.
